subject: E2E SLO matrix & test/demo plan
messages:
From: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>
To: Amanda Li <amanda@fastretail.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>, Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-12-12T14:02:00-08:00
Subject: E2E SLO matrix & test/demo plan

Hi Amanda — thanks again for the time today. Quick recap from our discovery so we have shared context and clear next steps. I pulled the notes into sections (pain points, current stack, success criteria, and next steps). Please flag anything I missed.

Pain points (what you told us)
- End users expect near-instant responses in the shopping assistant; current perceived latency is a conversion blocker.
- Peak concurrency at promotional drops creates sustained high tail latency (p95) and occasionally timeouts.
- Streaming UX: tokens arrive in large bursts rather than smoothly, which hurts perceived responsiveness on mobile.
- Cost: OpenAI-hosted runs are a material operational cost when scaled; caching has helped but is limited for personalization.

Current stack
- Frontend chat client -> FastRetail API -> requests to OpenAI + a small LRU prefix cache.
- No dedicated inference pool today; everything is on shared cloud endpoints.
- Observability: basic request/response latency traces and Prometheus metrics (not token-level breakdowns).

Success criteria (what FastRetail needs to consider a win)
- E2E p95 for assistant completions <= 250ms for single-turn queries under normal load, <= 350ms during 95th percentile promo traffic.
- Streaming semantics: first token < 120ms, then steady token cadence (no >200ms gaps) for median responses.
- Support 500 concurrent active users in a region with graceful degradation to a smaller-capacity model if capacity constrained.
- Maintain or reduce current per-session inference cost after optimization (target: <= 0.7x current).

Next steps / asks from Redwood
1) Schedule a 60m demo focused on end-to-end throughput/latency (propose Wed 12/15 11:00 PST or Thu 12/16 09:00 PST). We will bring: Marissa (SE) to run a live perf plan and share a demo harness.
2) If you can, attach a short SLO matrix (p95/p99 targets, measurement method) and an example prompt set + mean/median token lengths — Marissa will use these to size the test.
3) Share a small sample of traffic shape: concurrency profile across the day and an example peak-minute QPS. If any logs (sanitized) are available showing timeouts or tail latency spikes, those help.

Attachments: I’ve attached a proposed demo plan (redwood-demo-plan.pdf) and a template SLO matrix we can adapt.

Thanks — I’ll get Marissa on a follow-up once we lock the time.

—
Ben Carter

Ben — thanks for the clear summary, this is great and aligns with our internal notes. A couple of clarifications / additions:

- Our internal p95 target is measured end-to-end (client -> app -> inference -> client render). Network overhead is part of the budget.
- Typical response token lengths are 20–80 tokens for product questions; richer recommendations can be 200–400 tokens but are less frequent (roughly 10% of sessions).
- Peak profile: during a promotional drop we see short spikes: up to 150 req/s sustained for ~10 minutes, overall peak concurrent active users ~620 in us-west. Normal-day steady state is ~60 req/s.
- We already use a small prefix cache but it doesn’t help personalized flows. We are open to a hybrid routing strategy (fast small model for routing + larger model for personalization).

I attached our internal SLO_requirements_FastRetail.xlsx — it has the measured latency distribution and the customer impact notes. We’re happy to run a quick internal check on the proposed dates; Thu 12/16 09:00 PST looks preferable.

Also: procurement may want a ballpark quote for a dedicated inference queue and a managed rollback SLA ahead of the demo. Evans is looped for procurement/contract questions.

Best,
Amanda
Director of Product — Conversational Retail | FastRetail Inc.

Subject: Re: E2E SLO matrix & test/demo plan — SE checklist

Amanda / Ben — hi, Marissa here (SE). Quick pre-demo checklist so we can make the session concrete and hands-on. If you can drop these files into the Drive link (I added a folder) or email them back, we’ll be set: 

1) Example prompt set (20–30 prompts representative of conversational shopping + 5 personalization-heavy prompts).
2) Mean/median/max response token counts per category. You already gave ranges — having sample payloads helps.
3) Concurrency shape: a CSV with timestamped QPS for a representative promo day (1-minute granularity is fine).
4) Access: a short-lived API key or a staging endpoint we can hit (read-only) so we can run non-destructive synthetic tests. If that’s not possible, we can run purely synthetic traffic but having server-side traces will let us measure true e2e.
5) Any compliance guardrails we must respect during the demo (PII redaction, sample anonymization).

For the promo spike synthetic test I propose:
- Warm-up: 5 minutes at 40% target QPS
- Spike: 10 minutes at 100% target QPS (you mentioned 150 req/s) with evenly distributed concurrency
- Cool-down: 5 minutes at 30%
- Measure: server-side p50/p95/p99 for token latency, first-token time, token cadence (max inter-token gap), and overall CPU/GPU utilization on our side.

If you can confirm the first-token target (e.g., <120ms) and whether we should include a client-side emulation latency (~30ms) in E2E numbers, I’ll finalize the test harness.

I’ll also bring a short runbook for canary rollouts (A/B split, automatic fallback to smaller model variant) so you can see how Redwood would degrade gracefully under pressure.

—
